newsitem.title: DENMARK: Clinton says NATO aiming to save Bosnia peace.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says NATO aiming to save Bosnia peace.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Friday a new drive by NATO to arrest accused Bosnian war criminals was part of an overall attempt to salvage the Dayton peace accords.
"We basically believe that we have to make an effort to save the Dayton process," Clinton told reporters on Air Force One en route to Denmark from Romania.

Clinton acknowledged that the NATO-led peacekeeping efforts had entered a new phase aimed at implementing the accords agreed during intense negotiations in Dayton, Ohio -- including the arrest of war criminals.

Although the official mandate of the NATO units has been to arrest those indicted for crimes during Bosnia's bloody civil war, the unofficial policy has been to avoid becoming bogged down in police-like actions.
However, British forces on Thursday led raids in their sector of Bosnia that led to the arrest of one suspect. A second person died in a shootout rather than be captured.

British NATO troops on Thursday shot and killed Simo Drljaca, the former Serb police chief of the northwestern town of Prijedor, when he resisted arrest, and seized the local hospital director for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal. He is now jailed in The Hague.

Clinton said taking steps to strengthen the efforts of the NATO forces was discussed extensively in Madrid at the alliance's summit this week and earlier this month in the United States at a gathering of the seven industrial nations.

"What we admitted to ourselves (was)...there was too much focus being given to what happens in June of '98 (when the U.S. hopes to withdraw its troops) and too little focus being given to each of these other elements" of the agreement, Clinton said.

Clinton told reporters: "I think it would be a fair conclusion for you to draw that we made a commitment ... that every element should be given greater attention" -- including arms control, helping the infrastructure and economic development. He said the capture of suspected war criminals "obviously is, at the moment, the most compelling."
"It would be fair for you to conclude that we have decided we should try to save Dayton," Clinton said. "And to save Dayton, all the elements had to be implemented."

Clinton cautioned that the changes did not amount to a dramatic shift in policy. "It also would be wrong to conclude that there was a decision to basically totally reform the mission. This was clearly within the mission," he said.
The Los Angeles Times reported earlier this week that U.S. Special Forces and the CIA have prepared a secret plan to capture former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic.
Quoting U.S. intelligence sources, the Times said the plan was a response to Washington's growing concern that Karadzic was a major threat to long-term peace in former Yugoslavia.
